read.sections.0.heading.source: Schools are deciding how to use AI
read.sections.0.heading.back: Schools are deciding how to use AI

read.sections.0.text.source: AI chat tools can answer questions, explain ideas and even write whole essays. So schools and families face a new question: how should students use them? In 2023, UNESCO, the United Nations organisation for education, asked more than 450 schools and universities. Fewer than 1 in 10 had any guidance about these tools. Later that year, UNESCO wrote guidance for governments. It asked them to protect students' privacy and to set a minimum age, such as 13, for children talking with these chat tools on their own. This is advice, not a law. Each country and school makes its own rules.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI chat tools can answer questions, explain ideas and even write whole essays. So schools and families face a new question: how should students use these tools? In 2023, UNESCO, the UN organisation for education, asked more than 450 schools and universities. Fewer than 1 in 10 had any guidance about these tools. Later the same year, UNESCO wrote guidance for countries' governments. It asked them to protect students' privacy and to set a minimum age, for example 13, for children who chat with these chat tools alone. This is advice, not a law. Each country and school makes its own rules.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Nigeria: an AI tutor with teachers in the room
read.sections.1.heading.back: Nigeria: an AI tutor with teachers in the room

read.sections.1.text.source: In 2024, World Bank researchers tested an AI tutor in nine state schools in Benin City, Nigeria. The students were in their first year of senior secondary school, usually about 15 years old. For six weeks, they came to computer rooms after school, twice a week, to practise English with an AI chat tool. Teachers trained for the project started each session with a first question to ask the tool. Then they walked around, helping students stay on task. At the end, these students did better on an English test than similar students who were not chosen. The researchers say the result came from the whole programme, the tool and the teachers together.
read.sections.1.text.back: In 2024, World Bank researchers tested an AI tutor in nine state schools in Benin City, Nigeria. The students were in the first year of senior high school, usually about 15 years old. For six weeks, they came to computer rooms after school, twice a week, to practise English with an AI chat tool. Teachers trained for this programme started each session with a first question to ask the tool. Then they walked around, helping students stay focused on their task. At the end of the programme, these students did better on an English test than similar students who were not chosen. The researchers say the result came from the whole programme, that is, the tool and the teachers together.
read.sections.1.text.note: "Senior secondary school" is "sekolah menengah atas", which Indonesian learners know as SMA. "Project" is "program" here.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: In 2024, researchers tested an AI tutor in Nigeria. The students were about 15 years old. For six weeks, they came after school, twice a week. They practised English with an AI chat tool. Trained teachers started each session. They gave a first question to ask the tool. Then they helped students stay on task. At the end, they took an English test. They did better than students who did not take part. The tool and the teachers worked together, the researchers say.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: In 2024, researchers tested an AI tutor in Nigeria. The students were about 15 years old. For six weeks, they came after school, twice a week. They practised English with an AI chat tool. Teachers who had been trained started each session. The teacher gave a first question to ask the tool. Then the teachers helped students stay focused. At the end, those students took an English test. Their results were better than students who did not take part. The tool and the teachers worked together, the researchers say.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Türkiye: practice with a tool is not the same as learning
read.sections.2.heading.back: Türkiye: practising with a tool is not the same as learning

read.sections.2.text.source: In 2023, researchers worked with nearly 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at a high school in Türkiye. In four maths lessons, a teacher reviewed a topic, students did practice problems, and then they took a test with no books or computers. During practice, some students had only their books. Some had a chat tool that could give full answers. Others had a tutor version that gave hints, using answers and common mistakes written by their teachers. Both AI groups did much better in practice. But on the test alone, the full-answer group did worse than the books-only group. The tool had become a shortcut. The hint group did about as well as the books-only group. Each study was one subject in one place, so results elsewhere may differ.
read.sections.2.text.back: In 2023, researchers worked with nearly 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at a senior high school in Türkiye. In four maths lessons, a teacher went over a topic, students did practice problems, and then they took a test with no books or computers. During practice, some students used only books. Some had a chat tool that could give full answers. The other students had a tutor version that gave hints, using answers and common mistakes written by their teachers. Both AI groups did much better in practice. But on the test without help, the full-answer group did worse than the group that used only books. The tool had become a shortcut. The hint group did about as well as the group that used only books. Each study was about only one subject in one place, so results elsewhere may be different.
read.sections.2.text.note: "On the test alone" is "dalam tes tanpa bantuan" (on the test without help).

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Another study was in Türkiye, with nearly 1,000 high school students. In four maths lessons, students did practice problems. Then they took a test with no help. Some practised with only books. Some had a chat tool that gave full answers. Others had a tool that gave hints. Their teachers helped to make it. Both tool groups did well in practice. On the test alone, the full-answer group did worse. The tool was a shortcut. The hint group did about the same as the books group. Each study was one subject in one place.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Another study was done in Türkiye, with nearly 1,000 senior high school students. In four maths lessons, students did practice problems. Each study was about only one subject in one place.

watch.summary.source: This short cartoon is about AI chatbots. A chatbot is a computer program you can chat with in writing. It is a bit like sending messages to a person. The video explains what chatbots are and how they work. It also asks why many of them are made to sound like people. A chatbot can sound friendly and human. This can make it feel like a friend. It can also make its answers feel more true than they are. But a chatbot is not a person. It does not really know you, and it can be wrong. So notice how a chatbot makes you feel. And check what it says before you trust it.
watch.summary.back: This short cartoon is about AI chatbots. A chatbot is a computer program you can chat with in writing. It feels a little like sending messages to someone. The video explains what a chatbot is and how it works. It also asks why many chatbots are made to sound like humans. A chatbot can sound friendly and human-like. This can make it feel like a friend. It can also make its answers feel more true than they really are. But a chatbot is not a human. It doesn't really know you, and it can be wrong. So notice what you feel because of a chatbot. And check what it says before you trust it.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Don't ask learners whether or how they have used AI tools for schoolwork, and don't ask them to type questions into a real AI tool in class. UNESCO's 2023 guidance asks governments to set an age limit for children's independent conversations with generative AI tools; its press release names 13, and news reports said some argue for 16. It is advice to governments, not a law or a rule for every learning tool, and many learners are younger than 13. The pretend tool keeps everyone offline.

educatorNotes.1.source: The two studies, simplified (claims/DW11.md). Nigeria (De Simone and others, World Bank, 2025): a randomised trial in nine public schools in Benin City, Edo State, June to July 2024, with first-year senior secondary students (typically 15). Students chosen at random could attend twelve 90-minute after-school sessions (at most two a week) using Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4). Teachers had three days' training, began each session with a prompt, guided students without teaching directly and circulated to keep them on task; monitors supervised the sessions. On a pen-and-paper test at the end, gains were 0.31 standard deviations overall and 0.23 on English, with better end-of-year exams too. The authors say the whole programme, tool and teacher guidance together, drove the result; they can't separate the AI's part from the teacher guidance, and don't know how long it lasts or whether it works in other subjects. Türkiye (Bastani and others, PNAS 2025; design from the 2024 working paper): nearly 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at one large high school, autumn 2023; four 90-minute sessions covering about 15% of the year's maths; the AI was available only during practice, with a teacher present. With GPT-4 in practice, grades rose 48% (plain chat tool) and 127% (hint tutor built with teachers' solutions and common mistakes); on the closed-book test afterwards, the plain-tool group scored 17% lower than the books-only group, and the tutor group about the same. Neither study shows an effect for every learner, subject or tool.
educatorNotes.1.back: The two studies, simplified (claims/DW11.md). Nigeria (De Simone and colleagues, World Bank, 2025): a randomised trial in nine public schools in Benin City, Edo State, June to July 2024, with first-year senior high school students (usually aged 15). Students chosen at random could attend twelve 90-minute after-school sessions (at most twice a week) with Microsoft Copilot (GPT-4). Teachers had three days' training, began each session with a prompt, guided students without teaching directly and walked around to keep students focused; monitors supervised the sessions. On a written test at the end, gains were 0.31 standard deviations overall and 0.23 for English, and end-of-year exam results were also better. The authors say the whole programme, the tool and teacher guidance together, produced the effect; they can't separate the AI's part from the teacher guidance, and don't know how long the effect lasts or whether the programme works for other subjects. Türkiye (Bastani and colleagues, PNAS 2025; design from the 2024 working paper): nearly 1,000 students in grades 9 to 11 at one large senior high school, autumn 2023; four 90-minute sessions covering about 15% of a year's maths; the AI was available only in practice, with a teacher in the class. With GPT-4 in practice, grades rose 48% (plain chat tool) and 127% (hint tutor built with teachers' worked solutions and common mistakes); on the closed-book test afterwards, the plain-tool group scored 17% lower than the books-only group, and the tutor group about the same. No study shows an effect for every learner, subject or tool.
